title: Implement Trie Prefix Tree
statement: Build a Trie, a tree that stores words one letter per node. insert(word) adds a word. search(word) says whether exactly that word was inserted. startsWith(prefix) says whether any inserted word begins with the prefix. Words are lowercase letters.

example.caption: After inserting tea, ten and to, the letters t and e are stored once and shared. search(te) is false, startsWith(te) is true.

input.label: trie after insert tea, ten, to

output.label: startsWith(te) walks t, e and stops on a real node

idea.sentence: Words that start the same share the same first nodes, so every lookup just walks one letter at a time down from the root.

jargon.plain: A tree where each edge is one letter. A path from the root spells a prefix. Said like "try", from retrieval.
The first few letters of a word. "app" is a prefix of "apple".
A boolean on a node that says a stored word finishes here. It tells "app" the word apart from "app" the prefix of apple.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: the operation names, then their arguments, e.g. ["Trie","insert","search"], [[],["tea"],["tea"]]

vars.meaning: length of the word or prefix being used

compare.bruteLabel: Keep a list of words and scan it
compare.unit: steps per lookup, for a short word. The trie cost depends on L, not on n

rows.name: List of words
rows.note: search compares against words one by one. startsWith must test every word.

rows.name: Trie
rows.note: Each operation touches at most one node per letter. The number of stored words does not matter.

fast.takeaway: A trie trades some memory for lookups that cost only the length of the query, and it answers prefix questions that a hash set cannot.

stages.title: Empty root
stages.note: Make one empty root node. It stands for the empty prefix.

stages.title: Insert: walk and build
stages.note: For each letter, reuse the child if it exists, otherwise create it. Shared prefixes are stored once.

stages.title: Mark the word end
stages.note: After the last letter, set the end flag on that node.

stages.title: Lookup: follow letters
stages.note: Step to the child for each letter. If a child is missing, the walk fails right there.

stages.title: Decide
stages.note: search needs the end flag on the final node. startsWith only needs the path to exist.

edges.title: Prefix, not a word
edges.why: The path h-e-l-l exists, but no word ends there. Only the end flag makes it a word.

edges.title: Empty trie
edges.why: The root has no children, so the first step already fails. Nothing is created by a lookup.

edges.title: Stored word is longer
edges.why: The walk reaches the end of car, then needs a child s that does not exist.

edges.title: Inserting twice
edges.why: Every node already exists, so the second insert only sets the same flag again.

gotchas.text: search and startsWith walk the same path. The only difference is the last check: the end flag for search, nothing for startsWith. Forgetting the flag makes every prefix look like a word.
A plain object as the children map breaks on keys such as "constructor" or "__proto__", because they exist on every object already. A Map (or Object.create(null)) has no such keys.
A map field is nil until you make it. Writing to a nil map panics, so create children when you create the node: children: map[rune]*node{}.
map[rune]*node handles any letters. For lowercase only, a [26]*node array is faster and needs no make, but you must compute ch - 'a' for the index.
Ranging over a string gives runes, not bytes, so multi-byte letters are handled as whole characters.

recap.key: One node per letter, shared by every word with that prefix. A flag on a node marks a finished word.
recap.complexity: insert, search, startsWith O(L). Space O(total letters).
moves: Root node for the empty prefix
insert: reuse or create a child per letter, flag the last node
Lookup: follow letters, stop at the first missing child
search needs the flag, startsWith does not
